power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = c("p ≥ .271", "p ≥ .382", "p ≥ .163", 
"p ≥ .249"), Text = c("None of the rest-activity indicators was associated with sleep disturbance in the primary model, at either the between-person or the within-person level (Table 2; all p ≥ .271).", 
"With the symptom-only score (S8), no rest-activity indicator was associated with sleep disturbance (all p ≥ .382).", 
"No rest-activity indicator was associated with difficulty initiating sleep, nocturnal awakening, or frequent sleep medication use (all p ≥ .163).", 
"In the cumulativelogit model for the composite score, ORs ranged from 0.81 to 1.17 (all p ≥ .249)."
)), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"
))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. text.text: Purpose: To examine associations between accelerometer-derived rest-activity indicators and sleep disturbance among older adults.
Methods: This analysis included 1,373 person-wave observations from 569 National Health and Aging Trends Study participants.
Multilevel models separated within-person and between-person components of the least active five-hour period (L5), coefficient of variation, and behavioral fragmentation.
Relative amplitude (RA) was included at the between-person level in the primary model and examined separately in sensitivity analyses.

Results: In primary analyses, no rest-activity indicator was associated with sleep disturbance, including when sleep medication use was excluded; within-person estimates were small (95% CI bounds within ±0.031).
Weak between-person associations for L5 and RA emerged only in exploratory, model-dependent analyses.
Pain, depressive symptoms, chronic disease burden, and educational attainment were associated with sleep disturbance.
Conclusion: Rest-activity indicators showed no clear association with self-reported sleep disturbance, and small between-person estimates were model-dependent.
Health-related and socioeconomic factors warrant attention in population-based sleep research.

Sleep disturbance is common among community-dwelling older adults, with approximately one-third to one-half of adults aged 65 years and older reporting persistent difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep (Foley et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Sleep disturbance is common among community-dwelling older adults, with approximately one-third to one-half of adults aged 65 years and older reporting persistent difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Foley et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Sleep disruption is associated with adverse health outcomes (Medic et al., 2017), and insomnia has been linked to a higher risk of subsequent depression (Li et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Sleep disruption is associated with adverse health outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Medic et al., 2017)</ref>, and insomnia has been linked to a higher risk of subsequent depression <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Li et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Identifying factors associated with sleep disturbance remains an important priority in research on aging and health.
Age-related changes in circadian regulation and daily rest-activity organization may contribute to sleep difficulties in later life (Vitiello et al., 2004; Zitting & Yuan, 2025).
text.formatted: Age-related changes in circadian regulation and daily rest-activity organization may contribute to sleep difficulties in later life <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Vitiello et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Zitting & Yuan, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Daily rest-activity patterns reflect the temporal organization of behavior across periods of activity and rest.

The circadian system regulates the timing of sleep and wakefulness, providing a theoretical basis for investigating how daily behavioral rhythms relate to sleep disturbance (Roenneberg & Merrow, 2016).
text.formatted: The circadian system regulates the timing of sleep and wakefulness, providing a theoretical basis for investigating how daily behavioral rhythms relate to sleep disturbance <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Roenneberg & Merrow, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Wrist-worn accelerometers make it possible to characterize these patterns objectively in everyday settings, whereas self-reported activity measures may not adequately capture habitual behavior (VandeBunte et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Wrist-worn accelerometers make it possible to characterize these patterns objectively in everyday settings, whereas self-reported activity measures may not adequately capture habitual behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(VandeBunte et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Nonparametric measures of rest-activity rhythms include the least active five-hour period (L5), which reflects activity during the rest phase, and relative amplitude (RA), which represents the contrast between the most and least active periods (Van Someren et al., 1999).
text.formatted: Nonparametric measures of rest-activity rhythms include the least active five-hour period (L5), which reflects activity during the rest phase, and relative amplitude (RA), which represents the contrast between the most and least active periods <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Van Someren et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Behavioral fragmentation, measured using the active-to-sedentary transition probability (ASTP), captures the discontinuity of waking activity (Schrack et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Behavioral fragmentation, measured using the active-to-sedentary transition probability (ASTP), captures the discontinuity of waking activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Schrack et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Day-to-day variability in activity volume provides an additional dimension of behavioral organization.
These indicators characterize complementary aspects of daily activity patterns that may have different relationships with sleep disturbance.

Previous research has associated accelerometer-derived rest-activity indicators with physical function, cognition, and neuropsychiatric outcomes in older adults, including participants in the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS; Shim & Onnela, 2026).
text.formatted: Previous research has associated accelerometer-derived rest-activity indicators with physical function, cognition, and neuropsychiatric outcomes in older adults, including participants in the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Shim & Onnela, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Greater fragmentation of activity rhythms has also been linked to depression and anxiety in a population-based cohort (Luik et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Greater fragmentation of activity rhythms has also been linked to depression and anxiety in a population-based cohort <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Luik et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence directly concerning sleep disturbance remains limited.
A population-based cross-sectional study found greater rest-activity rhythm fragmentation among adults reporting poor subjective sleep quality (Oliveira et al., 2024).
text.formatted: A population-based cross-sectional study found greater rest-activity rhythm fragmentation among adults reporting poor subjective sleep quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Oliveira et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, longitudinal research examining the correspondence between rest-activity indicators and self-reported sleep difficulties in community-dwelling older adults remains scarce.

As wrist accelerometry is increasingly incorporated into population-based studies of older adults, clarifying its correspondence with self-reported sleep complaints may help researchers determine how rest-activity indicators should be interpreted alongside symptom reports when studying sleep-related health in later life.

Longitudinal observations provide an opportunity to distinguish between-person differences in rest-activity patterns from within-person fluctuations over time (Curran & Bauer, 2011; Rohrer & Murayama, 2023).
text.formatted: Longitudinal observations provide an opportunity to distinguish between-person differences in rest-activity patterns from within-person fluctuations over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Curran & Bauer, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Rohrer & Murayama, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Associations observed between individuals with different habitual activity patterns may not necessarily reflect associations between changes in activity patterns and sleep complaints within the same individual (Rohrer & Murayama, 2023).
text.formatted: Associations observed between individuals with different habitual activity patterns may not necessarily reflect associations between changes in activity patterns and sleep complaints within the same individual <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Rohrer & Murayama, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Separating these associations is important because estimates that combine within-person and between-person variation may obscure their respective contributions (Bell et al., 2019; Curran & Bauer, 2011).
text.formatted: Separating these associations is important because estimates that combine within-person and between-person variation may obscure their respective contributions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bell et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Curran & Bauer, 2011</ref>).

text.text: An additional analytic consideration is that rest-activity indicators may be correlated with one another.

Associations involving rhythm stability and sleep indicators with depression and anxiety in a population-based study were sensitive to adjustment for other rhythm and sleep measures (Luik et al., 2015), suggesting that estimates may depend on how correlated indicators are modeled.
text.formatted: Associations involving rhythm stability and sleep indicators with depression and anxiety in a population-based study were sensitive to adjustment for other rhythm and sleep measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Luik et al., 2015)</ref>, suggesting that estimates may depend on how correlated indicators are modeled.

text.text: The present study addresses these gaps using three waves of NHATS data, drawn from a nationally representative cohort of U.S. adults aged 65 years and older (Freedman & Kasper, 2019).
text.formatted: The present study addresses these gaps using three waves of NHATS data, drawn from a nationally representative cohort of U.S. adults aged 65 years and older <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Freedman & Kasper, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The study aimed to examine associations between accelerometer-derived rest-activity indicators and self-reported sleep disturbance and to distinguish between-person differences from within-person changes.
At the between-person level, we hypothesized that higher relative amplitude and lower behavioral fragmentation would be associated with fewer reported sleep problems.
Within-person associations and associations involving L5 and the coefficient of variation were examined without directional hypotheses.
probability sampling design anchored to the Medicare enrollment file, which covers approximately 96% of U.S. adults aged 65 years and older (Freedman & Kasper, 2019).

text.text: The study protocol was approved by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health Institutional Review Board (IRB No.
00002083; NHATS, n.d.), and all participants provided informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 2013).
text.formatted: 00002083; NHATS, n.d.), and all participants provided informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki <ref type="bibr">(World Medical Association, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Beginning in Round 11, participants in an accelerometer substudy wore an ActiGraph CentrePoint Insight Watch on the wrist continuously for approximately 7 days per wave (Schrack et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Beginning in Round 11, participants in an accelerometer substudy wore an ActiGraph CentrePoint Insight Watch on the wrist continuously for approximately 7 days per wave <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Schrack et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Waves were linked by unique participant identifiers.
The accelerometry sample was selected in Round 11 and followed through Round 14 (Van de Kerckhove et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The accelerometry sample was selected in Round 11 and followed through Round 14 (Van de <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Kerckhove et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Participants were eligible if they had valid accelerometer data (at least 4 valid wear days with at least 90% wear time per day) and complete data on sleep disturbance and all covariates.
Of 1,377 person-wave observations from 570 participants who met the accelerometer criteria, 4 observations with missing study variables were excluded.
The analytic sample comprised 1,373 observations from 569 participants (Round 12, n = 517; Round 13, n = 450; Round 14, n = 406).
Of these participants, 333 contributed three waves, 138 contributed two waves, and 98 contributed one wave.
Although NHATS includes adults aged 65 years and older, no participants aged 65-69 years were in the analytic sample, and consequently the youngest age category in the models was 70-74 years.
The analytic sample was defined by accelerometer participation and data completeness, and NHATS survey weights were not applied, so estimates describe the analytic sample rather than the population.
Rest-Activity Indicators.
Raw accelerometer signals were recorded at 64 Hz and processed into minute-level activity counts using standardized NHATS procedures implemented in the R package arctools (Karas et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Raw accelerometer signals were recorded at 64 Hz and processed into minute-level activity counts using standardized NHATS procedures implemented in the R package arctools <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Karas et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Nonwear was defined as at least 90 consecutive minutes with zero activity counts, and a valid wear day required at least 90% wear time (1,296 minutes), consistent with NHATS accelerometry processing guidelines (Schrack et al., 2022 (Schrack et al., , 2025)).
text.formatted: Nonwear was defined as at least 90 consecutive minutes with zero activity counts, and a valid wear day required at least 90% wear time (1,296 minutes), consistent with NHATS accelerometry processing guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Schrack et al., 2022</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Schrack et al., , 2025))</ref>.

text.text: Analyses used the revised accelerometry files that corrected time-zone misclassification affecting a subset of participants (Etzkorn et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Analyses used the revised accelerometry files that corrected time-zone misclassification affecting a subset of participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Etzkorn et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Extreme values of the accelerometerderived indicators were winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles.
Four indicators were derived from daily activity summaries.
L5 was the mean activity count during the least active five-hour interval across valid days.

RA was calculated as (M10 -L5)/(M10 + L5), following standard nonparametric analysis of rest-activity rhythms (Van Someren et al., 1999), where M10 is the mean activity during the most active 10-hour interval, so that higher values indicate greater contrast between the most and least active periods.
text.formatted: RA was calculated as (M10 -L5)/(M10 + L5), following standard nonparametric analysis of rest-activity rhythms <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Van Someren et al., 1999)</ref>, where M10 is the mean activity during the most active 10-hour interval, so that higher values indicate greater contrast between the most and least active periods.

text.text: The coefficient of variation (CV) of daily total activity characterizes day-to-day variability in activity volume.
L5 and CV were examined as complementary indicators of rest-phase activity and dayto-day variability.

Behavioral fragmentation was the ASTP, calculated as the number of transitions from an active minute (≥1,853 counts per minute; Koster et al., 2016) to a sedentary minute divided by the total number of active minutes in the day, averaged across valid days, following the calculation approach used in prior NHATS accelerometry research (Schrack et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Behavioral fragmentation was the ASTP, calculated as the number of transitions from an active minute (≥1,853 counts per minute; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Koster et al., 2016)</ref> to a sedentary minute divided by the total number of active minutes in the day, averaged across valid days, following the calculation approach used in prior NHATS accelerometry research <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Schrack et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Higher ASTP values indicate more fragmented waking activity.

Sleep disturbance was assessed with three NHATS items: difficulty falling asleep for 30 or more minutes (HC20), waking during the night with difficulty returning to sleep (HC21), and frequent use of sleep medication (HC22).
Each item was coded 0 (absent) or 1 (present).
The items were summed to a composite score from 0 to 3, with higher scores indicating more reported sleep-related problems (Foley et al., 2004).
text.formatted: The items were summed to a composite score from 0 to 3, with higher scores indicating more reported sleep-related problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Foley et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Because sleep medication use reflects treatment as well as symptoms, the composite indexes reported sleep-related problems rather than insomnia symptoms alone; a symptom-only score omitting the medication item was therefore also examined (S8).
The three items were also analyzed separately.

Because the recall period of the sleep items did not coincide with the 7-day accelerometer wear period, the analyses address correspondence between habitual rest-activity patterns and reported sleep problems rather than night-to-night associations.
Covariates.

All models adjusted for gender (male or female), race (White or non-White), educational attainment (high school or GED [reference], less than high school, some college, bachelor's degree, graduate degree), and age category (70-74 [reference], 75-79, 80-84, 85-89, 90 years and older), based on their established associations with sleep in older adults (Foley et al., 2004; Li et al., 2016; Mezick et al., 2008).
text.formatted: All models adjusted for gender (male or female), race (White or non-White), educational attainment (high school or GED <ref type="bibr">[reference]</ref>, less than high school, some college, bachelor's degree, graduate degree), and age category <ref type="bibr">(70-74 [reference]</ref>, 75-79, 80-84, 85-89, 90 years and older), based on their established associations with sleep in older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Foley et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Li et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Mezick et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Health covariates were chronic disease burden (count of self-reported physician-diagnosed conditions), pain (any pain in the preceding month), and depressive symptoms measured with the two-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-2; Kroenke et al., 2003).
text.formatted: Health covariates were chronic disease burden (count of self-reported physician-diagnosed conditions), pain (any pain in the preceding month), and depressive symptoms measured with the two-item Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-2; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Kroenke et al., 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Survey wave was included as a standardized continuous fixed effect.
Chronic disease count, PHQ-2, and survey wave were standardized directly (z scores), whereas the rest-activity indicators were standardized after decomposition.
The within-person and between-person decomposition was applied to the rest-activity indicators, which were the primary exposures.
The time-varying health covariates were entered without decomposition as adjustment variables, so their coefficients are not distinct within-person or between-person associations.

Rest-activity indicators were decomposed into within-person and between-person components using person-mean centering (Bell et al., 2019; Curran & Bauer, 2011; Rohrer & Murayama, 2023): the between-person component was each participant's mean across observed waves, and the within-person component was the deviation from that mean at each wave.
text.formatted: Rest-activity indicators were decomposed into within-person and between-person components using person-mean centering <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bell et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Curran & Bauer, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Rohrer & Murayama, 2023)</ref>: the between-person component was each participant's mean across observed waves, and the within-person component was the deviation from that mean at each wave.

text.text: Each component was standardized after decomposition, so coefficients refer to a one-standard-deviation difference.

Because L5 and RA were strongly correlated (r = -0.80), the within-person component of RA was omitted from the primary model, since adding it raised the VIF of within-person L5 from 1.01 to 4.99 (S5).

Both between-person components were retained to evaluate the hypothesized RA association, although they were also correlated (r = -0.78; VIF = 5.66 for L5 and 6.78 for RA), and models excluding each indicator (S6 and S7) were examined to address this overlap.
The primary model therefore included both components of L5, CV, and behavioral fragmentation and the betweenperson component of RA.

For each indicator, the ICC was obtained from an unconditional random-intercept model, and the within-person SD was the SD of deviations from the person mean across all observations, including the zero deviations of participants observed once.

Linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts were estimated by maximum likelihood in the R package lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) with the BOBYQA optimizer, and fixedeffect tests used the Satterthwaite approximation in the lmerTest package (Kuznetsova et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts were estimated by maximum likelihood in the R package lme4 <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Bates et al., 2015)</ref> with the BOBYQA optimizer, and fixedeffect tests used the Satterthwaite approximation in the lmerTest package <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Kuznetsova et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The null model provided the ICC of the outcome, marginal and conditional R² followed Nakagawa and Schielzeth (2013), and a likelihood ratio test compared the adjusted and null models.
text.formatted: The null model provided the ICC of the outcome, marginal and conditional R² followed <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Nakagawa and Schielzeth (2013)</ref>, and a likelihood ratio test compared the adjusted and null models.

text.text: Coefficients represent expected differences in the 0-3 sleep disturbance score per onestandard-deviation difference in the predictor.

Eight sensitivity analyses were conducted: (S1) excluding chronic disease burden, (S2) excluding PHQ-2, (S3) restricting to participants observed in all three waves, (S4) using a frequency-weighted sleep disturbance score (range 3-15), (S5) including both within-and between-person RA, (S6) excluding RA, (S7) excluding L5, and (S8) using a symptom-only score (HC20 plus HC21, range 0-2) that omits the sleep medication item.
S6-S8 and the itemlevel models were added after the primary results were examined and are exploratory.

The three sleep items were analyzed with population-averaged logistic models estimated by generalized estimating equations (GEE; Liang & Zeger, 1986) with an exchangeable working correlation and robust standard errors (geepack package; Højsgaard et al., 2006), since random-intercept logistic models were unstable, and the composite was also analyzed with a cumulative-logit mixed model (ordinal package; Christensen, 2023).
text.formatted: The three sleep items were analyzed with population-averaged logistic models estimated by generalized estimating equations (GEE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Liang & Zeger, 1986)</ref> with an exchangeable working correlation and robust standard errors (geepack package; <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Højsgaard et al., 2006)</ref>, since random-intercept logistic models were unstable, and the composite was also analyzed with a cumulative-logit mixed model (ordinal package; <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Christensen, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Results are reported as odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
Selective attrition was assessed by comparing baseline (Round 12) characteristics of participants who also contributed Round 14 data (completers) with those who did not (noncompleters).
Independent-samples t tests were used for continuous variables (rest-activity indicators and sleep disturbance), and chi-square tests were used for categorical variables (gender and race).
Tests were two-sided (α = .05) and not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
Model assumptions were checked with residual diagnostic plots.
All analyses were performed using R version 4.3.3 (R Core Team, 2024).
Table 1 presents descriptive characteristics of the analytic sample (N = 1,373 personwave observations from 569 participants).
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">1</ref> presents descriptive characteristics of the analytic sample (N = 1,373 personwave observations from 569 participants).

text.text: Women made up 53.8% of observations (739/1,373), and 85.5% (1,174/1,373) were White.
The most common age category was 75-79 years (45.2%), and 21.2% of observations were from participants aged 85 years or older.
Educational attainment was high, with 37.8% of observations from participants with a graduate degree and 4.5% from those with less than a high school education.
Pain was reported in 58.4% of observations.
The mean PHQ-2 score was 0.63 (SD = 0.94) and the mean number of chronic conditions was 2.83 (SD = 1.40).
The mean sleep disturbance score was 0.52 (SD = 0.76).
Scores of 0, 1, 2, and 3 occurred in 62.6%, 24.6%, 10.9%, and 1.9% of observations.
Difficulty initiating sleep, nocturnal awakening, and frequent sleep medication use were reported in 20.0%, 13.0%, and 19.0% of observations.
Mean values of the rest-activity indicators were 124.25 (SD = 75.87) for L5, 0.86 (SD = 0.08) for RA, 0.33 (SD = 0.08) for CV, and 0.30 (SD = 0.08) for behavioral fragmentation.
In the null model, the ICC was 0.593, indicating that 59.3% of the model-estimated variance in sleep disturbance was between persons, with the remaining 40.7% representing within-person variation.
The adjusted model fit better than the null model, χ²(21) = 87.98, p < .001.
text.formatted: The adjusted model fit better than the null model, χ²(21) = 87.98, p < .001.

text.text: The marginal R² was .088, the conditional R² was .586, and the adjusted ICC was .546.
The rest-activity indicators were stable across waves for L5, RA, and behavioral fragmentation (ICC = .72, .73, and .83) but not for CV (ICC = .18).
One within-person standard deviation of the observed deviations corresponded to 31.3 counts for L5 (41% of its total SD), 0.034 for RA, 0.056 for CV, and 0.027 for behavioral fragmentation.
Model-based within-person SDs were larger, at 41.1 counts for L5, 0.044 for RA, 0.074 for CV, and 0.036 for behavioral fragmentation.
None of the rest-activity indicators was associated with sleep disturbance in the primary model, at either the between-person or the within-person level (Table 2; all p ≥ .271).
text.formatted: None of the rest-activity indicators was associated with sleep disturbance in the primary model, at either the between-person or the within-person level (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>; all p ≥ .271).

text.text: The within-person estimates were small, with 95% CI bounds within approximately ±0.031 points on the 0-3 scale per standard-deviation change in L5, CV, or behavioral fragmentation.
The between-person estimates were less precise.

For example, each 1-SD higher between-person L5 corresponded to a 0.026-point higher sleep disturbance score (B = 0.026, 95% CI = [-0.096, 0.149]), and each 1-SD higher between-person RA to a 0.034-point lower score (B = -0.034, 95% CI = [-0.167, 0.100]), so bounds extended to approximately 0.17 points per standard deviation.
Pain (B = 0.114, p = .004), depressive symptoms (PHQ-2; B = 0.087, p < .001), and chronic disease burden (B = 0.070, p = .010) were associated with higher sleep disturbance.
text.formatted: Pain (B = 0.114, p = .004), depressive symptoms (PHQ-2; B = 0.087, p < .001), and chronic disease burden (B = 0.070, p = .010) were associated with higher sleep disturbance.

text.text: Compared with high school/GED, those without a high school diploma reported higher sleep disturbance (B = 0.355, p = .011), and those with a graduate degree reported lower sleep disturbance (B = -0.148, p = .030); other education categories did not differ significantly.
Gender, race, age category, and survey wave were not significantly associated with sleep disturbance, and the estimate for ages 80-84 relative to 70-74 was borderline (B = -0.156, p = .052).
Table 3 summarizes S1-S5, which were consistent with the primary model.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">3</ref> summarizes S1-S5, which were consistent with the primary model.

text.text: Excluding chronic disease burden (S1) or PHQ-2 (S2) did not change the pattern, and between-person RA remained nonsignificant in S2 (p = .555).
Restricting to three-wave participants (S3) and using the frequency-weighted score (S4) also produced no significant associations.
In S5, the withinperson RA estimate was negative but not significant (B = -0.059, SE = 0.032, p = .064).
Including both RA components raised the variance inflation factor (VIF) of within-person L5 from 1.01 to 4.99, and the VIF of within-person RA was 5.62.
Table 4 presents exploratory models in which weak between-person associations were observed when L5 and RA were examined separately.
text.formatted: Table <ref type="table">4</ref> presents exploratory models in which weak between-person associations were observed when L5 and RA were examined separately.

text.text: Without RA (S6), between-person L5 was weakly associated with more sleep disturbance (B = 0.054, SE = 0.027, 95% CI = [0.001, 0.107], p = .047).
Without L5 (S7), between-person RA was weakly associated with less sleep disturbance (B = -0.059, SE = 0.030, 95% CI = [-0.117, -0.001], p = .045).

These estimates correspond to about 7% to 8% of the outcome standard deviation per standard deviation of the indicator, and they were not independent since L5 and RA were strongly correlated at the between-person level (r = -0.78).

This study examined whether accelerometer-derived rest-activity indicators were associated with self-reported sleep disturbance among older adults participating in the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS).
Three findings are highlighted.

First, none of the indicators was associated with sleep disturbance in the primary analyses, at either the withinperson or the between-person level, and this pattern held when sleep medication use was excluded from the outcome; thus, the hypothesized associations for relative amplitude and behavioral fragmentation were not supported.

The within-person estimates were also small and precisely estimated (95% CI bounds within ±0.031 on the 0-3 scale per standard-deviation change), suggesting that large within-person associations are unlikely on the scale examined.

Second, small between-person associations for the least active five-hour period (L5) and relative amplitude (RA) appeared only in exploratory models that separated the two indicators, and they were model-dependent.
Third, pain, depressive symptoms, chronic disease burden, and educational attainment were more consistently associated with sleep disturbance.
Because the study was observational, these findings describe associations rather than causal effects.

The lack of consistent associations in the primary analyses, together with the precision of the within-person estimates, is notable given the growing evidence linking rest-activity organization to health outcomes in later life.

Previous studies have associated disrupted activity rhythms with depression and anxiety (Luik et al., 2015) and have identified relationships between accelerometer-derived rhythm characteristics and physical function, cognition, and neuropsychiatric outcomes in NHATS (Shim & Onnela, 2026).
text.formatted: Previous studies have associated disrupted activity rhythms with depression and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Luik et al., 2015)</ref> and have identified relationships between accelerometer-derived rhythm characteristics and physical function, cognition, and neuropsychiatric outcomes in NHATS <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Shim & Onnela, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These findings, however, concern different outcomes and study populations and do not necessarily imply that rest-activity indicators will be associated with self-reported sleep disturbance in a community-based sample.
One possible explanation for the present results lies in the distinction between the behavioral patterns captured by accelerometry and the subjective experience of sleep difficulties.

Although circadian processes contribute to the temporal regulation of sleep and wakefulness (Roenneberg & Merrow, 2016), measures derived from wrist movement primarily describe how activity and rest are distributed across daily life.
text.formatted: Although circadian processes contribute to the temporal regulation of sleep and wakefulness <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Roenneberg & Merrow, 2016)</ref>, measures derived from wrist movement primarily describe how activity and rest are distributed across daily life.

text.text: They do not directly assess endogenous circadian timing or the perceived quality of sleep.

Previous research has shown that self-reported and measured sleep duration are only modestly related (Lauderdale et al., 2008), with further variation in the correspondence between subjective and objective sleep quality among older adults (Vitiello et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Previous research has shown that self-reported and measured sleep duration are only modestly related <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Lauderdale et al., 2008)</ref>, with further variation in the correspondence between subjective and objective sleep quality among older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Vitiello et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the lack of consistent associations in this study may reflect differences in the aspects of sleep health captured by behavioral activity patterns and selfreported symptoms, rather than an absence of any relationship between circadian regulation and sleep.
Features of the outcome measure may also have limited the detection of associations.

Sleep disturbance was indexed by three binary items, yielding a score with only four possible values (0-3) on which most observations (62.6%) were 0, so modest differences in sleep may not have been registered.

Reported sleep problems were also relatively stable, with 59.3% of outcome variance lying between persons and item responses changing little across waves, leaving limited within-person variation for changes in rest-activity patterns to explain.
In addition, the recall period of the sleep items did not coincide with the 7-day accelerometer wear period.
Each of these features would be expected to attenuate associations, and sleep measures that are more finely graded and aligned in time with accelerometer wear would provide a stronger test.

The longitudinal findings also indicate that the level at which rest-activity patterns are examined matters for interpreting their relationship with sleep disturbance (Bell et al., 2019; Curran & Bauer, 2011).
text.formatted: The longitudinal findings also indicate that the level at which rest-activity patterns are examined matters for interpreting their relationship with sleep disturbance <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bell et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Curran & Bauer, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Within-person deviations in L5, day-to-day activity variability, and behavioral fragmentation were not accompanied by corresponding differences in reported sleep disturbance across the three annual assessments.
At the between-person level, associations involving L5 and RA emerged only in exploratory models in which the indicators were examined separately.

The direction of the RA association was consistent with the hypothesis, and the L5 association, for which no direction was predicted, was in the corresponding direction, with greater activity during the rest period and a weaker contrast between active and rest periods accompanying more sleep disturbance.
Their dependence on model specification, however, limits the evidence for distinct associations of either indicator with sleep complaints.

Because RA is calculated partly from L5 activity, the two measures share information about rest-activity organization, and their strong correlation in the present sample may have reduced the stability of their individual estimates when modeled simultaneously.
Prior population-based research has likewise shown that associations involving activity rhythms and sleep-related measures can be sensitive to adjustment for related indicators (Luik et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Prior population-based research has likewise shown that associations involving activity rhythms and sleep-related measures can be sensitive to adjustment for related indicators <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Luik et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The present findings therefore suggest that apparent associations between individual rhythm measures and sleep disturbance should be interpreted in relation to both their shared information and the source of variation being analyzed.
In particular, weak differences observed between individuals should not be assumed to characterize changes occurring within the same individual over time.
In contrast to the rest-activity indicators, pain, depressive symptoms, chronic disease burden, and educational attainment were associated with self-reported sleep disturbance.
Greater pain, depressive symptoms, and chronic disease burden were related to more sleep disturbance, whereas higher educational attainment was related to less.
Because observations from participants with less than a high school education represented only 4.5% of the analytic sample, education contrasts involving this group should be interpreted cautiously.

These associations are consistent with previous evidence linking sleep problems in later life to physical illness, psychological symptoms, and socioeconomic circumstances (Foley et al., 2004; Li et al., 2016; Mezick et al., 2008).
text.formatted: These associations are consistent with previous evidence linking sleep problems in later life to physical illness, psychological symptoms, and socioeconomic circumstances <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Foley et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Li et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Mezick et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: These findings indicate that health-related and socioeconomic characteristics remain relevant correlates of reported sleep disturbance even when multiple restactivity indicators are considered.
Nevertheless, the associations of pain and chronic disease burden were weaker when sleep medication use was excluded from the outcome.
This difference suggests that the observed relationships partly depend on the composition of the sleep disturbance measure.

Because medication use may reflect both the presence of sleep problems and their clinical management, combining medication use with symptom reports may capture a broader construct than sleep disturbance alone.

Strengths include repeated accelerometer assessments across three annual waves, explicit within-between decomposition (Bell et al., 2019; Curran & Bauer, 2011), multiple rest-activity indicators including behavioral fragmentation operationalized as the active-to-sedentary transition probability (Schrack et al., 2019), and sensitivity analyses that assessed the influence of correlated indicators and alternative definitions of sleep disturbance.
text.formatted: Strengths include repeated accelerometer assessments across three annual waves, explicit within-between decomposition <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bell et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Curran & Bauer, 2011)</ref>, multiple rest-activity indicators including behavioral fragmentation operationalized as the active-to-sedentary transition probability <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Schrack et al., 2019)</ref>, and sensitivity analyses that assessed the influence of correlated indicators and alternative definitions of sleep disturbance.

text.text: Attrition analyses indicated that participants who did not complete follow-up had lower CV and higher behavioral fragmentation at baseline.
These differences suggest possible selective attrition, although whether and in what direction attrition may have biased the observed associations remains uncertain.
This study has several limitations, organized into three areas.

First, regarding measurement: the sleep disturbance composite consisted of three coarse binary items whose recall period did not coincide with the accelerometer wear window, and the composite included sleep medication use, which may reflect treatment response rather than symptoms; more finely graded items temporally aligned with device wear would provide a stronger test.

Second, regarding design and sample: the rest-activity indicators capture observable behavior rather than endogenous circadian phase (which requires direct physiological assessment); the analytic sample was predominantly White and highly educated and analyses did not apply NHATS accelerometry weights, so findings reflect associations within the analytic sample rather than population estimates; additionally, only 4.5% of observations came from participants with less than a high school education, so comparisons involving that group should be interpreted with caution; participants who did not complete follow-up differed from completers in baseline activity variability and fragmentation, indicating possible selective attrition; and three annual observations may not capture shorter-term relationships between daily activity and sleep.

Third, regarding analytic considerations: limited within-person variation in individual sleep items constrained GEE analyses; the strong correlation between L5 and RA made their between-person effects sensitive to model specification; the relatively low stability of CV across waves raises questions about how well the person-level mean represents a stable individual characteristic; and exploratory analyses were conducted without adjustment for multiple comparisons in an observational design that precludes causal inference.
Future research should examine rest-activity organization alongside subjective sleep complaints, objective sleep characteristics, and direct measures of circadian phase.

Such assessments could help determine whether the weak associations observed here reflect differences between behavioral and subjective measures or variation in the physiological processes underlying sleep.

More frequent repeated measurements would also allow investigation of whether changes in rest-activity patterns are related to sleep difficulties over shorter intervals than those captured by annual assessments.

Given the sensitivity of the exploratory findings to model specification, careful consideration of correlations among rhythm indicators and separation of within-person and between-person associations will remain important in longitudinal research.
For population-based research on aging, these findings suggest that wrist accelerometryderived rest-activity summaries should not be treated as substitutes for directly reported sleep complaints.

They may provide complementary information about daily behavioral organization, but their limited correspondence with the sleep items examined here underscores the importance of retaining symptom-based assessments.
Pain, depressive symptoms, chronic disease burden, and educational attainment also warrant attention when investigating sleep-related health in later life.
